title: Speedrun
alt: Usain Bolt holds the world record in the 100 meter speedrun.
transcript:
[Cueball is sitting at a desk with a laptop, typing on it. Megan is standing behind him.]
Cueball: Aw man, Speedrun.com removed my world record just because I listened to Lateralus and Ænima to get in the flow.
Megan: Oh, a copyright thing?
Cueball: No, they don't allow Tool-assisted speedruns.
explanation:
is the sport of completing a  or a goal within a game (for example, completing the main story) as fast as possible. Speedrun.com is a popular leaderboard aggregator for speedrunners.

Apparently, Cueball's world-record setting attempt at some achievement was deleted from Speedrun.com because of the music he was listening to at the time. Megan makes the natural assumption that this was because the submission violated copyright on the music in question. It is common for video streamers to include a music 'bed', which can cause copyright issues if they have not taken care that their selections are cleared for use in this way. However, it turns out that his attempt was removed for being 'tool-assisted'. 

Cueball was apparently considered to have been assisted by (listening to) :  and  are albums by the band Tool. The comic was posted exactly 25 years after the Lateralus album was released.

A  (or TAS for short) is a type of speedrun where supplementary tools are used to manipulate inputs frame-by-frame to perfect a run. Such tools are mostly used for experimenting with new strategies or finding areas where a time can be optimized, but it is possible to cheat by passing off a tool-assisted run as a normal speedrun. The use of music as a concentration aid is generally not against the rules of the speedrun, unless the music serves as a makeshift , where it could be controversial in games relying on some sort of rhythm or precision. In real life, any problems caused by the use of copyrighted music during a speedrun would probably arise on the site hosting the video evidence (YouTube and Twitch, who are obligated to flag videos with copyright claims) rather than the site hosting the leaderboards (Speedrun.com).

The comic may be referencing ’s ascent of the  tower, during which he listened to Tool.

The title text is another pun, this time on the word "speedrun". 's world record-setting 100-meter dash record is a "speedrun" in the sense that it is literally a speedy run, and also an attempt by someone to complete a task as fast as possible. It is very common for internet personalities to say they are 'speedrunning' when they are doing a task quickly, even when completely unrelated to gaming (e.g. speedrunning petting a cat).  The notion of such a record being classified as a legitimate speedrun isn't farfetched as Speedrun.com has some leaderboards for In Real Life records. The use of "speedrun" to refer to an actual fast run may be considered to be a case of 3123: Canon.

In road races like s, wearing technical devices is severely restricted. For example, according to Book C2.1 rule 6.3.2 of Book of Rules of World Athletics they are not allowed to transmit any data. Under rule 6.3.2 CD, radio and similar devices are not allowed, so it would be very hard to find device which is allowed for speedrunning a marathon while listening to Lateralus and/or Ænima, as many devices that are able to play audio would probably have functions similar to CD and/or radio. Even if they don't have those functions, in serious competitions, athletes are checked for wearing earphones or headphones (though amateurs get some leeway and can even carry their mobile phones). Even if it was allowed, pro athletes wouldn't want to carry any additional weight to be able to listen to music, as even reducing weight of shoes can significantly improve your time, so any audio play back device would add weight which they would want to avoid.

It is possible that speedrunning was on Randall's mind due to the recent social media trend of , in which someone attempts to get as deep as they can into a building belonging to the  before being kicked out.
